analysis.one_liner: Makes federal agencies prove rules' costs outweigh benefits and lets courts easier strike major regulations down.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 20, 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill has no cosponsors and no committee or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the core rules that govern how federal agencies write regulations. For every significant rule — anything with a $100 million-plus economic impact, higher consumer prices, or effects on health and safety — agencies would have to run formal cost-benefit analyses, consider multiple alternatives, and adopt whichever option 'maximizes net benefits,' with a White House regulatory office (OIRA) approving both proposed and final versions. It lengthens the comment process, makes agency guidance formally non-binding, and changes judicial review so courts decide legal questions themselves rather than deferring to agency expertise, while shielding OIRA's own decisions from court challenge. The practical effect is to make major federal protections — on workplace safety, air and water, food and drug safety, financial rules — slower to issue, easier to challenge, and more likely to be written around the least costly option for regulated companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated companies and industry trade groups. They gain multiple extended comment rounds, a legal default toward the cheapest regulatory option, and stronger grounds to sue in court over any rule they dislike. Smaller procedural gains go to the public: dockets, plain-language rule summaries, and publication of industry-agency contacts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated corporations and industry trade groups

how_it_helps.text: For any 'major rule' — one costing the economy $100 million or more, raising prices significantly, or affecting health, safety, competition, or employment — agencies must adopt the alternative that maximizes net benefits, counting cumulative regulatory costs and only benefits that fall within the rule's authorizing statute, unless a new OIRA Administrator approves a different choice.

Agencies must publish an advance notice at least 90 days before proposing a major rule, hold comment periods of at least 60 days (90 for major rules) plus a 30-day window to respond to other commenters, and follow a published timetable, with reports to Congress for missed deadlines.

Both proposed and final rules must be submitted to the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for review before publication, and actions of that Administrator are largely exempted from judicial review.

Courts reviewing rules would decide questions of law 'de novo' — on their own rather than giving weight to the agency's reading — review the whole record, and could remand rules without striking them down.
Agency guidance would carry an on-page statement that it does not have the force of law, and 'major guidance' would need its own cost-benefit justification.
Each major rule would get a published assessment framework and periodic retrospective assessments (no more than 10 years apart) examining whether the rule should be modified or repealed.

Some provisions do add public-facing transparency: rule information placed in public dockets, a 100-word plain-language summary posted on regulations.gov, and publication of ex parte contacts between agencies and stakeholders who may benefit from a rule.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost as slower, weaker, and more litigation-prone federal protections: workplace safety, air and water quality, food and drug safety, consumer finance, and similar rules would take longer to issue, be constrained to the cheapest compliance option, and be easier to overturn in court. Federal agencies would absorb heavy new analytical and procedural burdens, and public-interest groups without corporate-scale legal budgets would be at a disadvantage in the longer, more formal process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal health, safety, and financial protections

drawbacks.text: Requiring agencies to pick the net-benefit-maximizing alternative for major rules — counting only benefits within the rule's own statute and cumulative regulatory costs — pushes agencies toward the least protective option that clears the cost test, and unquantifiable harms like lost lives or degraded environments are hard to weigh in that formula.

Deciding legal questions de novo and reviewing the whole record invites well-funded regulated parties to relitigate rules in court, while the same bill largely blocks judicial review of OIRA's own decisions, the office with the new gatekeeping power.

Layered notice, comment, response, and timetable requirements would add months or years to rulemaking, delaying urgent protections in public health and safety emergencies except where agencies invoke a 'good cause' exception they would have to justify in writing.
Agencies and federally funded groups would be barred from publicly advocating for or against their own proposed rules, limiting agencies' ability to explain to the public why a protection is needed.

The bill's defenders would argue agencies already perform cost-benefit analysis under existing executive orders and that formalizing it, extending comment periods, and adding retrospective reviews protects against overregulation and improves accountability — a good-faith position, though the bill goes well beyond current practice by making cost-optimization a legal mandate enforceable in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency pieces — public dockets, plain-language summaries, publication of industry contacts with agencies — are real and worth having. But the bill's core is a set of procedural and legal hurdles whose weight falls unevenly: a corporation with a large legal team can work a 90-day comment period, three alternatives, and a de novo court challenge far more easily than the public whose protections are being delayed or diluted. The honest weighing is that the process costs are borne by everyone who depends on federal rules, while the litigation and negotiating leverage accrues to concentrated interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on May 20, 2025, and has sat there since, with no cosponsors and no committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Beth Van Duyne introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No member of either party has signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action — no committee markup, vote, or floor consideration — appears in the bill's action history after the referral.
If enacted, the bill's changes would apply only to rulemakings started after enactment, not to pending or completed rules.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has had to give anything up: because the bill has not advanced, existing rules and the current rulemaking process remain untouched. If it later passed, the clear winners would be regulated industries that face federal rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; existing rules and process unchanged

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee markup or any consideration since its referral on May 20, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the sponsor is a Republican with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record yet, though past regulatory-overhaul bills have generally drawn mostly Republican support.

industries.industry: Large regulated corporations (manufacturing, energy, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, finance)
industries.note: The bill gives them extended comment windows, a legal default toward the cheapest-to-comply rule, and easier court challenges to any major rule. What they save in compliance and litigation comes out of the strength of the protections the public gets from those rules.

industries.industry: Corporate law firms and trade associations
industries.note: De novo review of legal questions, whole-record review, and remand-without-vacatur create more avenues to challenge rules, and the layered comment process multiplies opportunities for organized industry input.

Agencies would face heavy new analysis, OIRA pre-publication review, communication restrictions, and retrospective assessment duties, while their legal interpretations lose weight in court — all of which diminishes their capacity to protect the public.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action months after referral, standalone passage is very unlikely this session. Pieces of it could resurface attached to a larger deregulation or appropriations package, but on its current path it will probably remain in committee.
